claim: E2F transcription factors play a critical role in controlling cell fate.
source: The E2F transcription factors play a critical role in controlling cell fate.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that establishes the known role of E2F proteins.

claim: In Drosophila, the inactivation of E2F in either muscle or fat body results in lethality.
source: In Drosophila, the inactivation of E2F in either muscle or fat body results in lethality, suggesting an essential function for E2F in these tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript and references previous work.

claim: E2F regulates carbohydrate metabolism in muscle and fat body.
source: The proteomic profiling of E2F-deficient muscle and fat body revealed that E2F regulates carbohydrate metabolism, a conclusion further supported by metabolomic profiling.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the proteomic and metabolomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Animals with E2F-deficient fat body had a lower level of circulating trehalose.
source: Intriguingly, animals with E2F-deficient fat body had a lower level of circulating trehalose and reduced storage of fat.
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of trehalose in hemolymph shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Animals with E2F-deficient fat body had reduced storage of fat.
source: Intriguingly, animals with E2F-deficient fat body had a lower level of circulating trehalose and reduced storage of fat.
evidence: This is supported by lipid droplet size measurements and triglyceride content shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: A sugar supplement was sufficient to restore both trehalose and fat levels in E2F-deficient fat body animals.
source: Strikingly, a sugar supplement was sufficient to restore both trehalose and fat levels, and subsequently rescued animal lethality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of trehalose levels (Figure 6D) and triglyceride content (Figure 6G) on high sugar diet.

claim: A sugar supplement rescued lethality of animals with E2F-deficient fat body.
source: Strikingly, a sugar supplement was sufficient to restore both trehalose and fat levels, and subsequently rescued animal lethality.
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: E2F loss exerts both tissue-intrinsic and systemic effects.
source: Here, we show that the E2F loss exerts both tissue-intrinsic and systemic effects.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple experiments showing effects in both the tissue where E2F is depleted and in distant tissues.

claim: The activity of E2F1 is restrained by the retinoblastoma protein pRB.
source: The activity of E2F1 is restrained by the retinoblastoma protein pRB, a tumor suppressor that is either mutated or functionally inactivated in various cancers (Dyson, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: pRB is a tumor suppressor that is either mutated or functionally inactivated in various cancers.
source: The activity of E2F1 is restrained by the retinoblastoma protein pRB, a tumor suppressor that is either mutated or functionally inactivated in various cancers (Dyson, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate pRB, releasing E2F1 to activate the expression of genes that regulate DNA synthesis, S-phase entry, and mitosis.
source: In the textbook description of E2F regulation, the cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate pRB, releasing E2F1 to activate the expression of genes that regulate DNA synthesis, S-phase entry, and mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical E2F/pRB pathway.

claim: E2Fs have additional roles that extend beyond the cell cycle.
source: Several studies have shown that E2Fs have additional roles that extend beyond the cell cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: E2F can act as a regulator of cellular metabolism.
source: Notably, E2F can also act as a regulator of cellular metabolism (Denechaud et al., 2017; Nicolay and Dyson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: E2F1 was implicated in global glucose homeostasis by controlling insulin secretion in the pancreatic beta cells.
source: E2F1 was implicated in global glucose homeostasis by controlling insulin secretion in the pancreatic beta cells (Annicotte et al., 2009) and it is needed to promote adipogenesis (Fajas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E2F1 is needed to promote adipogenesis.
source: E2F1 was implicated in global glucose homeostasis by controlling insulin secretion in the pancreatic beta cells (Annicotte et al., 2009) and it is needed to promote adipogenesis (Fajas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E2F1 and pRB form repressor complexes on the promoters of genes involved in oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: E2F1 and pRB have been shown to form repressor complexes on the promoters of genes involved in oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis (Blanchet et al., 2011), and E2F1 has been found to activate the expression of glycolytic and lipogenic genes in the liver (Denechaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E2F1 activates the expression of glycolytic and lipogenic genes in the liver.
source: E2F1 and pRB have been shown to form repressor complexes on the promoters of genes involved in oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis (Blanchet et al., 2011), and E2F1 has been found to activate the expression of glycolytic and lipogenic genes in the liver (Denechaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The inactivation of the RB pathway results in profound metabolic alterations, including changes in central carbon metabolism that confer sensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: Accordingly, the inactivation of the RB pathway results in profound metabolic alterations, including changes in central carbon metabolism that confer sensitivity to oxidative stress (Nicolay et al., 2013; Reynolds et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms of action of pRB and E2F orthologues are highly conserved from flies to mammals.
source: The mechanisms of action of pRB and E2F orthologues are highly conserved from flies to mammals (van den Heuvel and Dyson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila E2F family contains two E2F genes, E2f1 and E2f2.
source: The Drosophila E2F family contains two E2F genes, E2f1 and E2f2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila genetics.

claim: Each E2F forms a heterodimer with the binding partner Dp, which is required for high-affinity DNA binding.
source: Each E2F forms a heterodimer with the binding partner Dp, which is required for high-affinity DNA binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E2F/Dp function.

claim: Dp is encoded by a single gene in Drosophila.
source: An important feature of the Drosophila E2F/RB network is that Dp is encoded by a single gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila genetics.

claim: The entire program of E2F regulation can be abolished by the inactivation of Dp.
source: As a result, the entire program of E2F regulation can be abolished by the inactivation of Dp, either through a Dp mutation or in a tissue-specific manner by RNA interference (RNAi) (Frolov et al., 2005; Guarner et al., 2017; Royzman et al., 1997; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The loss of E2F function, as seen in Dp mutants, is permissive for development until pupation when lethality occurs.
source: The loss of E2F function, as seen in Dp mutants, is permissive for development until pupation when lethality occurs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hallmarks of E2F regulation, such as cell proliferation, differentiation, or apoptosis, were largely unaffected in Dp mutants.
source: Surprisingly, hallmarks of E2F regulation, such as cell proliferation, differentiation, or apoptosis, were largely unaffected in Dp mutants (Frolov et al., 2001; Royzman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inactivation of E2F in the fat body phenocopied the lethal phenotype of Dp mutants.
source: Interestingly, the inactivation of E2F in either the fat body, which serves the roles of liver and adipose tissue, or muscles phenocopied the lethal phenotype of Dp mutants pointing to the requirement of E2F for animal viability in both tissues (Guarner et al., 2017; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inactivation of E2F in muscles phenocopied the lethal phenotype of Dp mutants.
source: Interestingly, the inactivation of E2F in either the fat body, which serves the roles of liver and adipose tissue, or muscles phenocopied the lethal phenotype of Dp mutants pointing to the requirement of E2F for animal viability in both tissues (Guarner et al., 2017; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The fat body serves the roles of liver and adipose tissue in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, the inactivation of E2F in either the fat body, which serves the roles of liver and adipose tissue, or muscles phenocopied the lethal phenotype of Dp mutants pointing to the requirement of E2F for animal viability in both tissues (Guarner et al., 2017; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila biology.

claim: The lethality of Dp mutants can be rescued by tissue-specific expression of Dp in either the muscles or fat body.
source: The lethality of Dp mutants can be rescued by tissue-specific expression of Dp in either the muscles or fat body (Guarner et al., 2017; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The loss of Dp in fat body does not impact muscle development.
source: The loss of E2F/DP in the fat body does not impact muscle development
evidence: This is supported by data showing no difference in VL3 muscle area between cg>RFP and cg>Dp-RNAi (Figure 1A-B).

claim: The area of the VL3 muscles in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals were significantly smaller than control.
source: As previously reported, the area of the VL3 muscles in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals were significantly smaller than control (Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: No differences were detected in the VL3 muscle area between cg>RFP and cg>Dp-RNAi larval muscles.
source: In contrast, no differences were detected in the VL3 muscle area between cg>RFP and cg>Dp-RNAi larval muscles (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by measurements shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The inactivation of Dp in fat body is accompanied by an increase in DNA damage response that leads to the appearance of binucleated cells.
source: Second, fat body-specific Dp depletion triggers a reduction in fat storage and an increase in DNA damage response that promotes uncontrolled DNA replication and, ultimately, leads to the occurrence of binucleated cells (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: The depletion of Dp driven by the fat body-specific GAL4 driver cg-GAL4 resulted in the formation of binucleated cells (~4.2% in cg>Dp-RNAi).
source: We confirmed that the depletion of Dp driven by the fat body-specific GAL4 driver cg-GAL4 resulted in the formation of binucleated cells (~4.2% in cg>Dp-RNAi, Figure 2A–B) while none were found in fat bodies from wild-type animals.
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: No binucleated cells were found in fat bodies from wild-type animals.
source: We confirmed that the depletion of Dp driven by the fat body-specific GAL4 driver cg-GAL4 resulted in the formation of binucleated cells (~4.2% in cg>Dp-RNAi, Figure 2A–B) while none were found in fat bodies from wild-type animals.
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The binucleated cell phenotype was observed in E2f2; E2f1 double mutant animals.
source: This phenotype was also observed in E2f2; E2f1 double mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and in Dp null mutants (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation.

claim: The binucleated cell phenotype was observed in Dp null mutants.
source: This phenotype was also observed in E2f2; E2f1 double mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and in Dp null mutants (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The occurrence of binucleated cells in fat body were observed in Lpp>DpRNAi larva.
source: The occurrence of binucleated cells in fat body were also observed in Lpp>DpRNAi larva (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which died at pupa stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), thus confirming the cell-autonomous effect of Dp loss in fat body, in concordance with previous work (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lpp>DpRNAi animals died at pupa stage.
source: The occurrence of binucleated cells in fat body were also observed in Lpp>DpRNAi larva (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which died at pupa stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), thus confirming the cell-autonomous effect of Dp loss in fat body, in concordance with previous work (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablation of Dp in muscles led to the appearance of binucleated cells (7.7% in Mef2>Dp-RNAi).
source: Surprisingly, ablation of Dp in muscles led to the appearance of binucleated cells (7.7% in Mef2>Dp-RNAi, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Only cg>Dp-RNAi fat bodies showed reduced levels of Dp protein.
source: We confirmed that Dp was depleted in a tissue-specific manner, as only cg>Dp-RNAi fat bodies showed reduced levels of Dp protein as revealed by immunofluorescence using anti-Dp antibodies (Figure 2A, bottom panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The MRN proteins were not recruited in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals.
source: Notably, the MRN proteins were not recruited in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals, as opposed to cg>Dp-RNAi fat body cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The loss of Dp in muscles elicits defects in fat body that might be similar to the phenotype seen in Dp-deficient fat body albeit not accompanied by the upregulation of MRN proteins.
source: We conclude that the loss of Dp in muscles elicits defects in fat body that might be similar to the phenotype seen in Dp-deficient fat body albeit not accompanied by the upregulation of MRN proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat bodies without MRN recruitment.

claim: Dp-deficient muscle exerts a systemic effect on normal tissues, such as fat body.
source: Thus, Dp-deficient muscle seems to exert a systemic effect on normal tissues, such as fat body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that muscle-specific Dp depletion causes defects in fat body.

claim: The cg-GAL4 driver is expressed in the fat body.
source: G-TRACE showed that the cg-GAL4 driver is expressed in the fat body in agreement with previous report (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by G-TRACE data in Figure 3A and citation.

claim: No GFP or RFP signal was detected in larval muscles with cg-GAL4, suggesting that at no point during development cg-GAL4 was expressed in muscles.
source: No GFP or RFP signal was detected in larval muscles (Figure 3A, right panel) suggesting that at no point during development cg-GAL4 was expressed in muscles.
evidence: This is supported by G-TRACE data in Figure 3A.

claim: Mef2-GAL4 expression was detected in larval skeletal and smooth muscles and in the adult muscle precursors (wing disc myoblasts), but not in the fat body.
source: Similarly, Mef2-GAL4 expression was detected in larval skeletal and smooth muscles (Figure 3B, left panels), and in the adult muscle precursors (wing disc myoblasts), but not in the fat body (Figure 3B, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by G-TRACE data in Figure 3B.

claim: The Dp::GFP was efficiently depleted in fat body of cg>Dp-RNAi compared to control.
source: The Dp::GFP was efficiently depleted in fat body of cg>Dp-RNAi compared to control (Figure 3C, quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The levels of the Dp::GFP remained unaffected in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi.
source: Importantly, the levels of the Dp::GFP remained unaffected in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi (Figure 3C, quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Staining with anti-Dp antibody showed no changes in the endogenous expression of Dp in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi.
source: This result was further confirmed by staining with anti-Dp antibody that showed no changes in the endogenous expression of Dp in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The expression of Dp::GFP in muscles was not altered in cg>Dp-RNAi.
source: Similarly, the expression of Dp::GFP in muscles was not altered in cg>Dp-RNAi, whereas, as expected, Dp::GFP was significantly reduced in muscles of Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control (Figure 3F, quantified in Figure 3G).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Dp::GFP was significantly reduced in muscles of Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control.
source: Similarly, the expression of Dp::GFP in muscles was not altered in cg>Dp-RNAi, whereas, as expected, Dp::GFP was significantly reduced in muscles of Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control (Figure 3F, quantified in Figure 3G).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The endogenous levels of Dp protein in muscles did not change upon Dp depletion in the fat body.
source: Using anti-Dp antibody, we further confirmed that the endogenous levels of Dp protein in muscles did not change upon Dp depletion in the fat body (Figure 3F, quantified in Figure 3H).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3F and 3H.

claim: The occurrence of binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body is not due to altered expression of Dp in fat body of these animals.
source: Thus, the occurrence of binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body is not due to altered expression of Dp in fat body of these animals and, therefore, reflects a systemic effect induced by muscle-specific Dp depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing no change in Dp levels in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals.

claim: The occurrence of binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body reflects a systemic effect induced by muscle-specific Dp depletion.
source: Thus, the occurrence of binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body is not due to altered expression of Dp in fat body of these animals and, therefore, reflects a systemic effect induced by muscle-specific Dp depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing binucleated cells in fat body without local Dp depletion.

claim: 7.1% of cells in fat body of Dp mutants were binucleated.
source: In agreement with previously published data (Guarner et al., 2017), 7.1% of cells in fat body of Dp mutants were binucleated and this phenotype was fully rescued in the Dp-/-; cg>Dp animals (Figure 4A, quantified in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B and citation.

claim: The binucleated phenotype in Dp mutant fat body was fully rescued in the Dp-/-; cg>Dp animals.
source: In agreement with previously published data (Guarner et al., 2017), 7.1% of cells in fat body of Dp mutants were binucleated and this phenotype was fully rescued in the Dp-/-; cg>Dp animals (Figure 4A, quantified in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The binucleated phenotype was largely rescued by re-expression of Dp in muscles of Dp mutants, in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp animals.
source: Strikingly, the binucleated phenotype was also largely rescued by re-expression of Dp in muscles of Dp mutants, in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp animals (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Fat bodies of Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp animals still contained fragmented and decondensed/large nuclei indicating that the rescue was incomplete.
source: We note, however, that fat bodies of Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp animals still contained fragmented and decondensed/large nuclei indicating that the rescue was incomplete.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Staining with anti-Dp antibody confirmed the lack of Dp expression in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp fat bodies.
source: Staining with anti-Dp antibody confirmed the lack of Dp expression in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp fat bodies (Figure 4A, bottom panel), thus excluding the possibility of a leaky expression of Mef2-GAL4 driver in the fat body.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Muscle-specific expression of Dp can rescue the binucleated phenotype of Dp mutant fat body.
source: Thus, muscle-specific expression of Dp can rescue the binucleated phenotype of Dp mutant fat body, which is consistent with the idea that E2F/Dp in muscle exerts a systemic effect in larva that impacts the fat body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The expression of Dp in the fat body was insufficient to suppress the small size of VL3 muscles in Dp-/- mutant larvae.
source: In contrast, the expression of Dp in the fat body was insufficient to suppress the small size of VL3 muscles in Dp-/- mutant larvae (Figure 4C, quantified in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: VL3 muscle area was smaller in Dp-/- mutant larvae and fully rescued in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp.
source: As previously reported, VL3 muscle area was smaller in Dp-/- mutant larvae and fully rescued in Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp (Figure 4C, quantified in Figure 4D; Zappia and Frolov, 2016).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D and citation.

claim: E2F/Dp modifies the inter-tissue communication between muscle and fat body.
source: This suggests that E2F/Dp modifies the inter-tissue communication between muscle and fat body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the asymmetric rescue patterns observed.

claim: 6578 proteins were identified in fat body samples.
source: In the proteomics datasets, we identified and quantified 6578 proteins in fat body and 5370 proteins in muscle samples.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: 5370 proteins were identified in muscle samples.
source: In the proteomics datasets, we identified and quantified 6578 proteins in fat body and 5370 proteins in muscle samples.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: The intensity level of Dp protein was downregulated in both Dp-/- fat bodies and Dp-depleted muscles compared to the control tissues.
source: We confirmed that the intensity level of Dp protein was downregulated in both Dp-/- fat bodies and Dp-depleted muscles compared to the control tissues, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The expression levels of the well-known E2F-direct targets that are repressed by E2F, such as Arp53D, SpnE, and dATM, were upregulated in both Dp-/- fat bodies and Dp-depleted muscles.
source: Concordantly, the expression levels of the well-known E2F-direct targets that are repressed by E2F, such as Arp53D, SpnE, and dATM, were upregulated in both Dp-/- fat bodies and Dp-depleted muscles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A set of 5024 proteins were shared between fat body and muscle tissues.
source: A set of 5024 proteins that were shared between both tissues was selected for integrative analysis (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: The two proteomic datasets showed a Pearson correlation of r = 0.172.
source: These two datasets showed a Pearson correlation of r = 0.172 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) indicating that a relevant subset of the changes detected in fat body were also present in muscles.
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing the two datasets.

claim: 556 proteins increased and 456 proteins decreased in Dp-/- fat bodies.
source: We found that 556 proteins increased and 456 proteins decreased in Dp-/- fat bodies, whereas 844 increased and 1208 proteins decreased in Dp-depleted muscles (these are visualized in heatmaps in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: 844 proteins increased and 1208 proteins decreased in Dp-depleted muscles.
source: We found that 556 proteins increased and 456 proteins decreased in Dp-/- fat bodies, whereas 844 increased and 1208 proteins decreased in Dp-depleted muscles (these are visualized in heatmaps in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Categories related to DNA repair, glutathione metabolism, and amino acid metabolism were significantly enriched for upregulated proteins in both tissues.
source: Categories related to DNA repair, glutathione metabolism, and amino acid metabolism were significantly enriched for upregulated proteins in both tissues, while nucleotide metabolism was only significantly enriched in muscle (FDR<5%, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, top panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Nucleotide metabolism was only significantly enriched in muscle among upregulated proteins.
source: Categories related to DNA repair, glutathione metabolism, and amino acid metabolism were significantly enriched for upregulated proteins in both tissues, while nucleotide metabolism was only significantly enriched in muscle (FDR<5%, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, top panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Proteins related to cytochrome p450 enzymes that catalyze detoxification and biosynthetic reactions in fat body were upregulated in Dp mutants.
source: Additionally, proteins related to cytochrome p450 enzymes that catalyze detoxification and biosynthetic reactions in fat body (Chung et al., 2009) were upregulated in Dp mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, top panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the proteomic data and citation.

claim: The fat body proteome was enriched for pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid metabolism among downregulated proteins.
source: Among the downregulated proteins, the fat body proteome was enriched for pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid metabolism, whereas citrate cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and ribosome categories were significantly overrepresented among the muscle proteome upon the loss of Dp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, bottom panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Citrate cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and ribosome categories were significantly overrepresented among the muscle proteome upon the loss of Dp among downregulated proteins.
source: Among the downregulated proteins, the fat body proteome was enriched for pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid metabolism, whereas citrate cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and ribosome categories were significantly overrepresented among the muscle proteome upon the loss of Dp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, bottom panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: The upregulated proteins in Dp-deficient fat body and muscle showed a significant enrichment for DNA damage, DNA recombination, and homologous recombination.
source: As expected, the upregulated proteins in Dp-deficient fat body and muscle showed a significant enrichment for DNA damage, DNA recombination, and homologous recombination (Figure 5D, top panel, FDR < 5%).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation clustering analysis of shared proteomic changes.

claim: The top annotation cluster for downregulated proteins displayed a significant enrichment for glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and carbohydrate metabolic process.
source: The top annotation cluster for downregulated proteins displayed a significant enrichment for glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and carbohydrate metabolic process (Figure 5D, bottom panel, FDR < 5%), thus indicating that the loss of Dp alters carbohydrate metabolism in both fat body and muscle.
evidence: This is based on functional annotation clustering analysis of shared proteomic changes.

claim: The loss of Dp alters carbohydrate metabolism in both fat body and muscle.
source: The top annotation cluster for downregulated proteins displayed a significant enrichment for glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and carbohydrate metabolic process (Figure 5D, bottom panel, FDR < 5%), thus indicating that the loss of Dp alters carbohydrate metabolism in both fat body and muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional annotation clustering analysis.

claim: Fifty-five compounds showed significant changes in the Dp mutant compared to both controls (FDR < 5%).
source: Fifty-five compounds showed significant changes in the Dp mutant compared to both controls (FDR < 5%, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomic analysis.

claim: The major metabolic pathways that showed significant enrichment for downregulated compounds were glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ammonia recycling.
source: Interestingly, the major metabolic pathways that showed significant enrichment for downregulated compounds were glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ammonia recycling (FDR < 5%, Figure 5F, Supplementary file 7), which is largely consistent with the proteome analysis described above.
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the metabolomic data.

claim: Four metabolites of the core module of the glycolytic pathway (2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid, 3-phosphoglycerate, D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, and phosphoenolpyruvate) were significantly reduced in Dp mutant compared to both controls.
source: Notably, four metabolites of the core module of the glycolytic pathway, (Figure 5G), 2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid, 3-phosphoglycerate, D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, and phosphoenolpyruvate, were significantly reduced in Dp mutant compared to both controls (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is directly supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The tissue-specific depletion of Dp results in extensive metabolic changes in both fat body and muscle.
source: We conclude that the tissue-specific depletion of Dp results in extensive metabolic changes in both fat body and muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and metabolomic profiling data.

claim: E2F-depleted tissues undergo significant changes in carbohydrate metabolism affecting, in particular, glycolytic metabolites.
source: The alterations indicate that E2F-depleted tissues undergo significant changes in carbohydrate metabolism affecting, in particular, glycolytic metabolites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and metabolomic profiling data.

claim: Mef2>Dp-RNAi or cg>Dp-RNAi animals did not survive on control diet and died at pupal and pharate stage.
source: As expected, Mef2>Dp-RNAi or cg>Dp-RNAi did not survive on control diet and died at pupal and pharate stage (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The survival of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals was unaffected by different nutrient composition.
source: Interestingly, while the survival of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals was unaffected by different nutrient composition (Figure 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), cg>Dp-RNAi were highly sensitive to dietary changes.
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: cg>Dp-RNAi animals were highly sensitive to dietary changes.
source: Interestingly, while the survival of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals was unaffected by different nutrient composition (Figure 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), cg>Dp-RNAi were highly sensitive to dietary changes.
evidence: This is supported by viability data under different dietary conditions.

claim: The increase in protein content had a negative impact on the survival of cg>Dp-RNAi and resulted in significant developmental delay.
source: The increase in protein content had a negative impact on the survival of cg>Dp-RNAi and resulted in significant developmental delay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: About 83% of cg>Dp-RNAi animals showed melanotic masses at larval stages when reared on high protein diet.
source: About 83% of animals showed melanotic masses at larval stages when reared on high protein diet, and only 35% of third instar larva progressed onto pupa stages and eventually died (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Reducing the content of protein suppressed the occurrence of melanotic masses in cg>Dp-RNAi animals.
source: However, reducing the content of protein suppressed the occurrence of melanotic masses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D) and consequently increased their survival rate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C-D.

claim: Increasing lipid content up to 1% in diet was beneficial for survival as about 22% of cg>Dp-RNAi pupa reached adulthood.
source: In contrast, increasing lipid content up to 1% in diet was beneficial for survival as about 22% of cg>Dp-RNAi pupa reached adulthood (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No cg>Dp-RNAi animals survived on control diet (7.9% carbohydrates).
source: Strikingly, while no cg>Dp-RNAi animals survived on control diet (7.9% carbohydrates), almost half of them eclosed when reared in the presence of 12% carbohydrates and the lethality was fully rescued when food contained even higher amount of carbohydrates (16% or 24%) (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Almost half of cg>Dp-RNAi animals eclosed when reared in the presence of 12% carbohydrates.
source: Strikingly, while no cg>Dp-RNAi animals survived on control diet (7.9% carbohydrates), almost half of them eclosed when reared in the presence of 12% carbohydrates and the lethality was fully rescued when food contained even higher amount of carbohydrates (16% or 24%) (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi was fully rescued when food contained 16% or 24% carbohydrates.
source: Strikingly, while no cg>Dp-RNAi animals survived on control diet (7.9% carbohydrates), almost half of them eclosed when reared in the presence of 12% carbohydrates and the lethality was fully rescued when food contained even higher amount of carbohydrates (16% or 24%) (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The rescue of cg>Dp-RNAi lethality by high sugar diet was confirmed using a second fat body-specific driver r4-GAL4.
source: This result was confirmed using a second fat body-specific driver r4-GAL4 (Figure 6A, right panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The levels of Tps1 proteins were significantly reduced in Dp mutant fat body.
source: We noted that the levels of Tps1 proteins were significantly reduced in Dp mutant fat body, along with other enzymes that generate glucose-6P including phosphoglucomutase, glucose-6-phosphate isomerase, and hexokinase_A in the proteomic datasets (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Trehalase, an enzyme that converts trehalose back to glucose, was significantly increased in Dp-deficient fat body.
source: Additionally, trehalase, an enzyme that converts trehalose back to glucose, was significantly increased in Dp-deficient fat body.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Trehalose was significantly reduced in hemolymph of cg>Dp-RNAi larva compared to matching control when animals were reared on control diet.
source: Notably, trehalose was significantly reduced in hemolymph of cg>Dp-RNAi larva compared to matching control (Figure 6D) when animals were reared on control diet.
evidence: This is directly supported by trehalose measurement data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Switching to high sugar diet significantly improved the levels of trehalose in cg>Dp-RNAi to levels comparable to cg>mCherry-RNAi larva that were fed a control diet.
source: Switching to high sugar diet significantly improved the levels of trehalose in cg>Dp-RNAi to levels comparable to cg>mCherry-RNAi larva that were fed a control diet (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly supported by trehalose measurement data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The levels of circulating trehalose were largely unchanged in Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control.
source: In contrast, the levels of circulating trehalose were largely unchanged in Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly supported by trehalose measurement data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Dp mutants have lipid droplets of reduced and irregular size.
source: Dp mutants were previously shown to have lipid droplets of reduced and irregular size (Guarner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In control diet, Dp-depleted fat bodies displayed smaller lipid droplet size compared to control.
source: In control diet, Dp-depleted fat bodies displayed smaller lipid droplet size compared to control (Figure 6F, quantification in bottom panel), which is indicative of defects in fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This is directly supported by lipid droplet size measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid synthesis, was significantly reduced in fat body of cg>Dp-RNAi compared to control.
source: Concordantly, the expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid synthesis, was significantly reduced in fat body of cg>Dp-RNAi compared to control (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Feeding control larva a high sugar diet resulted in significantly larger lipid storage droplets.
source: As expected (Musselman et al., 2011; Pasco and Léopold, 2012), feeding control larva a high sugar diet resulted in significantly larger lipid storage droplets (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is directly supported by lipid droplet size measurements shown in Figure 6F and citations.

claim: Feeding cg>Dp-RNAi animals on high sugar diet dramatically improved the lipid droplet size in comparison to control diet.
source: Nevertheless, feeding cg>Dp-RNAi animals on high sugar diet dramatically improved the lipid droplet size in comparison to control diet.
evidence: This is supported by lipid droplet size measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The levels of triglycerides normalized to total protein content were significantly reduced in cg>Dp-RNAi animals reared on control diet compared to cg>mCherry-RNAi.
source: The levels of triglycerides normalized to total protein content were significantly reduced in cg>Dp-RNAi animals reared on control diet compared to cg>mCherry-RNAi.
evidence: This is directly supported by triglyceride measurement data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The normalized levels of triglycerides were fully restored in cg>Dp-RNAi animals fed on high sugar diet.
source: Moreover, the normalized levels of triglycerides were fully restored in cg>Dp-RNAi animals fed on high sugar diet.
evidence: This is directly supported by triglyceride measurement data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Muscle-specific Dp depletion did not affect either the size of lipid droplets in the fat body or the total content of triglycerides in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals.
source: In contrast, muscle-specific Dp depletion did not affect either the size of lipid droplets in the fat body or the total content of triglycerides in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 6H, respectively).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 6H.

claim: There were no major defects in glycogen storage normalized to protein content in cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control animals fed either a control or a high sugar diet.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G, there were no major defects in glycogen storage normalized to protein content in cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi compared to control animals fed either a control or a high sugar diet.
evidence: This is directly supported by glycogen measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Binucleated cells were readily found in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae fed a control diet.
source: Binucleated cells were readily found in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae fed a control diet, but the phenotype was not modified by rearing larvae on high sugar diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: The binucleated phenotype was not modified by rearing larvae on high sugar diet.
source: Binucleated cells were readily found in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae fed a control diet, but the phenotype was not modified by rearing larvae on high sugar diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: The essential function of Dp in fat body is to maintain homeostasis of the circulating sugar trehalose and to regulate fat storage.
source: Since dietary changes suppress the defects and fully rescue animal lethality, we infer that the essential function of Dp in fat body is to maintain homeostasis of the circulating sugar trehalose and to regulate fat storage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments with high sugar diet.

claim: The binucleated phenotype is most likely distinct from the metabolic defects.
source: The fact that binucleated cells persisted in the fat body of rescued animals suggests that the binucleated phenotype is most likely distinct from the metabolic defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that high sugar diet rescues lethality but not the binucleated phenotype.

claim: Dp loss causes extensive metabolic changes in both muscle and fat body.
source: It is clear from the molecular profiles that Dp loss causes extensive metabolic changes in both muscle and fat body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and metabolomic profiling data.

claim: E2F/Dp participates in the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism in both tissues.
source: The profiles indicate that E2F/Dp participates, in particular, in the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism in both tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteomic and metabolomic profiling data.

claim: The lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi could be rescued by increasing dietary sugar.
source: Such extensive changes to cellular metabolism likely have biological significance in both contexts, but we know that this is certainly true when Dp is depleted in the fat body because the lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi could be rescued by increasing dietary sugar.
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The fat body functions as a key sensor of the nutritional status and it couples systemic growth and metabolism with nutritional availability.
source: In Drosophila, the fat body functions as a key sensor of the nutritional status and it couples systemic growth and metabolism with nutritional availability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila fat body function.

claim: The lethality associated with cg>Dp-RNAi may stem from an imbalance between energy production and systemic growth.
source: The lethality associated with cg>Dp-RNAi may, therefore, stem from an imbalance between energy production and systemic growth.
evidence: This is speculation based on the metabolic defects observed and the known function of fat body.

claim: Carbohydrate metabolism defects in cg>Dp-RNAi larvae are consistent with studies of mammalian E2F1 in liver and adipose tissue.
source: Carbohydrate metabolism defects in cg>Dp-RNAi larvae are consistent with studies of mammalian E2F1 in liver and adipose tissue, tissues that metabolize nutrients and stores reserves of lipid and glycogen.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work in mammalian systems.

claim: E2F1 was shown to be required for the regulation of glycolysis and lipid synthesis in hepatocytes.
source: E2F1 was shown to be required for the regulation of glycolysis and lipid synthesis in hepatocytes (Denechaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: E2F1 was implicated in the regulation of PPARγ, the master adipogenic factor, during early stages of adipogenesis in adipose tissue.
source: In﻿ adipose tissue, E2F1 was implicated in the regulation of PPARγ, the master adipogenic factor, during early stages of adipogenesis (Fajas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The gene encoding for the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4, a key nutrient sensor and modulator of glucose oxidation, is directly regulated by E2F1.
source: Moreover, ﻿the gene encoding for the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4, a key nutrient sensor and modulator of glucose oxidation, and ﻿6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, a glycolytic enzyme, are directly regulated by E2F1 (Fernández de Mattos et al., 2002; Hsieh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The gene encoding for 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, a glycolytic enzyme, is directly regulated by E2F1.
source: Moreover, ﻿the gene encoding for the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4, a key nutrient sensor and modulator of glucose oxidation, and ﻿6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, a glycolytic enzyme, are directly regulated by E2F1 (Fernández de Mattos et al., 2002; Hsieh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A major function for the fat body is to control whole-animal sugar homeostasis.
source: A major function for the fat body is to control whole-animal sugar homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila fat body function.

claim: Trehalose and glucose metabolism plays a key role in regulating systemic energy homeostasis.
source: Interestingly, trehalose and glucose metabolism plays a key role in regulating systemic energy homeostasis (Matsuda et al., 2015; Yasugi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proper trehalose homeostasis is required for adapting animals to various dietary conditions.
source: Proper trehalose homeostasis is required for adapting animals to various dietary conditions, as evidenced by Tps1 mutants, which do not survive in low sugar diet (Matsuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tps1 mutants do not survive in low sugar diet.
source: Proper trehalose homeostasis is required for adapting animals to various dietary conditions, as evidenced by Tps1 mutants, which do not survive in low sugar diet (Matsuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The lethality associated with Mef2>Dp-RNAi was not rescued by altering the diet.
source: In contrast with cg>Dp-RNAi, the lethality associated with Mef2>Dp-RNAi was not rescued by altering the diet.
evidence: This is directly supported by viability data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The appearance of binucleated cells in the fat bodies of Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae demonstrates that the muscle-specific knockdown of Dp does have systemic effects.
source: However, the appearance of binucleated cells in the fat bodies of Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae demonstrates that the muscle-specific knockdown of Dp does have systemic effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of binucleated cells in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals.

claim: The mechanisms leading to the formation of binucleates in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals may differ from cg>Dp-RNAi and Dp-/- mutants since they are not associated with a DNA damage response.
source: We note that the mechanisms leading to the formation of binucleates in Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals may differ from cg>Dp-RNAi and Dp-/- mutants (Guarner et al., 2017) since they are not associated with a DNA damage response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of MRN protein recruitment in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat bodies.

claim: The binucleated cells in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals may be a symptom of stress.
source: Indeed, the binucleated cells in the fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals may be a symptom of stress; evidence for paracrine signals from muscle support this idea (Demontis et al., 2014; Demontis and Perrimon, 2009; Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work on muscle-fat body communication.

claim: The tissue-specific depletion of Dp causes systemic effects in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae.
source: We infer that the tissue-specific depletion of Dp causes systemic effects in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae, but it is particularly evident in cg>Dp-RNAi animals, which have a low level of circulating trehalose in hemolymph.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the various systemic effects observed.

claim: The level of circulating trehalose is a net result of the amount of trehalose released to hemolymph by fat body and its consumption by other organs, including rapidly growing muscles.
source: The level of circulating trehalose is a net result of the amount of trehalose released to hemolymph by fat body and its consumption by other organs, including rapidly growing muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trehalose metabolism in Drosophila.

claim: The trehalose requirement of wild-type organs in cg>Dp-RNAi animals may provide an additional challenge to the Dp-deficient fat body to maintain trehalose homeostasis.
source: The trehalose requirement of wild-type organs in cg>Dp-RNAi animals may provide an additional challenge to the Dp-deficient fat body to maintain trehalose homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the metabolic defects observed.

claim: The reduced demand for trehalose by Dp-deficient organs in the Dp-/- mutants may shift the balance toward increased levels of circulating trehalose.
source: Conversely, the reduced demand for trehalose by Dp-deficient organs in the Dp-/- mutants may shift the balance toward increased levels of circulating trehalose.
evidence: This is speculation about metabolic balance in whole-body mutants.

claim: The severity of the phenotype may differ between the whole-body Dp-/- mutant and the tissue-specific Dp inactivation.
source: Thus, one implication of our work is that the severity of the phenotype may differ between the whole-body Dp-/- mutant and the tissue-specific Dp inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in metabolic balance between whole-body and tissue-specific mutants.

claim: There is growing evidence of the systemic effects that muscles exert in different settings, including development and aging.
source: There is growing evidence of the systemic effects that muscles exert in different settings, including development and aging (Demontis et al., 2014; Demontis et al., 2013; Demontis and Perrimon, 2009; Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myokines are thought to be the main mediators of the inter-tissue communication between muscles and fat body, and other distant tissues.
source: Myokines are thought to be the main mediators of the inter-tissue communication between muscles and fat body, and other distant tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle-tissue communication.

claim: Dp-deficient muscle causes the appearance of binucleated cells in the distant fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae.
source: Here, we report that Dp-deficient muscle causes the appearance of binucleated cells in the distant fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi larvae.
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The fat body phenotype in Mef2>Dp-RNAi is due to the tissue-specific loss of Dp in muscles.
source: Our data strongly argue that the fat body phenotype is due to the tissue-specific loss of Dp in muscles as the levels of Dp remain unchanged in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body compared to control animals.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no change in Dp levels in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals (Figure 3).

claim: Maintaining proper homeostasis of triglyceride metabolism at an organismal level requires the orchestration of elaborated endocrine mechanism for inter-tissue communication.
source: Maintaining proper homeostasis of triglyceride metabolism at an organismal level requires the orchestration of elaborated endocrine mechanism for inter-tissue communication (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Myokines and other cytokines communicate systemic changes in nutrient sensing status and energy substrate storage via cross talk with insulin and Akt signaling pathway.
source: ﻿Myokines and other cytokines communicate systemic changes in nutrient sensing status and energy substrate storage via cross talk with insulin and Akt signaling pathway (Demontis et al., 2013; Géminard et al., 2009; Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The finding that Dp mutant animals develop to the late pupal stages and largely without defects was surprising.
source: Since E2F/DP proteins are master regulators of cell proliferation, the finding that Dp mutant animals develop to the late pupal stages and largely without defects was surprising.
evidence: This is a reflection on previous findings in the field.

claim: 20% of the proteins quantified in fat bodies were expressed at statistically different levels following tissue-specific Dp knockdown.
source: Indeed, 20% and 51% of the proteins that we quantified in fat bodies and muscles, respectively, were expressed at statistically different levels following tissue-specific Dp knockdown.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: 51% of the proteins quantified in muscles were expressed at statistically different levels following tissue-specific Dp knockdown.
source: Indeed, 20% and 51% of the proteins that we quantified in fat bodies and muscles, respectively, were expressed at statistically different levels following tissue-specific Dp knockdown.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Dp inactivation exerts a systemic effect and may impact distant wild-type tissues.
source: The second conclusion of our work is that Dp inactivation exerts a systemic effect and may impact distant wild-type tissues, which was completely missed in previous analysis of whole-body Dp mutants and became only evident when Dp was inactivated in a tissue-specific manner.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the tissue-specific experiments.

claim: Dp-deficient muscles induce mild defects in distant fat body.
source: We report that Dp-deficient muscles induce mild defects in distant fat body, while downregulation of Dp in fat body results in low level of circulating trehalose, which is likely the main cause of lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the various experiments showing systemic effects.

claim: Downregulation of Dp in fat body results in low level of circulating trehalose, which is likely the main cause of lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi animals.
source: We report that Dp-deficient muscles induce mild defects in distant fat body, while downregulation of Dp in fat body results in low level of circulating trehalose, which is likely the main cause of lethality of cg>Dp-RNAi animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with high sugar diet.

claim: The Dp mutant phenotype is a complex combination of both tissue-intrinsic and systemic effects.
source: Thus, the Dp mutant phenotype is a complex combination of both tissue-intrinsic and systemic effects.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the work.
